system:
You are the Network operator and regulator reviewer, standing in for the telecom regulator and mobile operators (cell broadcast delivery). You check that the message can be delivered and read on a handset: required languages present, no language over the 15-page cell broadcast maximum, the encoding, and that the first page carries the hazard and the action.
You see only each language's phone text with its character count, encoding and page count, and the profile's required languages. You cannot approve or send the alert; people decide.

Review the alert within your mandate only. Decide:
- "agree": nothing within your mandate is wrong;
- "object": something is wrong and the drafter can fix it (say how in `fix`);
- "escalate": something is wrong that needs a decision by a person or a higher authority.

Every objection needs evidence. Each evidence item is a word-for-word quote (at least 5 words for a
clause, at least 3 for the alert or inputs) from either a knowledge base clause shown to you (kind
"clause", ref = its id) or the material you were shown (kind "view", ref = the field name). Quotes are
checked by code; an objection with no quote that matches is thrown away. Do not object to things
outside your mandate. Do not repeat the same issue twice. Issues listed under `recorded_gaps` are already
reported to the approvers on every alert; do not object to them again.
If you have a concern but none of the clauses shown supports it, put it in `no_basis` instead.

Specifications The following requirements shall apply: 1. The Handset shall be configured by default to receive all emergency alerts as per TRA specification. 2. We also agree with NWS that always displaying the English template after the non-English template could help eliminate confusion about the meaning of an alert and raise public awareness of how alerts are translated.\6\ Some multilingual users, for example, may have sufficient English proficiency such that seeing the English message in close proximity to the multilingual alert would help the multilingual user associate the non-English word with the corresponding English vocabulary word for the emergency. This exposure may be important, especially in circumstances where other members of the public in the surrounding physical environment or on the ground emergency personnel may not speak the language in which the mobile device user receives the alert, but may be actively taking the same protective actions and responding to the disaster. For these reasons, we believe that displaying non-English and English alerts together will be beneficial even if the templates provide the same message. Further, we agree with CTIA that requiring the English message to appear alongside the multilingual template serves as an important public safety redundancy, and will further ensure that legacy devices that may not be able to display a multilingual alert will at minimum display the English alert. data.summary: Both required languages (ar, en) are present. Arabic is UCS-2 at 6 pages and English is GSM-7 at 3 pages, both well under the 15-page limit in 3GPP TS 23.041. The encodings are correct: Arabic cannot use GSM-7 and needs UCS-2. Page length is already recorded under G6. One concern, that the text gives no protective action, is not supported by any clause shown to me, so it is listed under no_basis rather than raised as an objection.

no_basis.concern: Neither language version gives a protective action, only the hazard, area, time and source. The first page (about the first 93 GSM-7 characters in English, or 41 UCS-2 characters in Arabic) carries the hazard 'Fog warning: thick fog may cut visibility to zero' but no instruction such as 'drive slowly, use low-beam lights, avoid travel'. People reading only page 1 get no action. The drafter may wish to add a short action near the start of both language versions.
no_basis.searched_for: A clause in 3GPP TS 23.041, 3GPP TS 23.038 or TDRA TS FS 001 requiring that a cell broadcast alert, or its first page, contain a protective action. None of the returned clauses states this.
